article_text:
The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre, and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs0.03 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs392.66 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.82 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 14 (Wednesday).

The price of HSD has come down from apeak of Rs520.35recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price hadpeaked at Rs458.41on April 3 after beginning itsupward trajectoryfrom Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government hasreintroduceda raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malikannouncedthat fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcingweekly revisionsto fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April alsoannouncedtargeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Tuesday that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs, while vowing no leniency for hoarders, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

PM Shehbaz chaired the first National Agricultural and Food Security Council (NAFSC) meeting in Islamabad today, according to a statement issued by the PMO.

Addressing the meeting, the prime minister said that wheat was available in abundant quantities to meet domestic needs.

“No leniency will be shown to those hoarding wheat,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying. “It is essential to determine the fair price of wheat before sowing so that farmers receive appropriate compensation for their labour.”

“We want farmers to get the fair price for wheat and for consumers to have affordable wheat,” he added.

The premier stated that the decision regarding the price of wheat would be made in consultation with the provinces.

“The consultation with the provinces will be completed soon, and the price of wheat will be announced shortly,” he said.

The prime minister further termed agriculture the “backbone of the national economy” and said it could set Pakistan’s economy on the path to growth in the short term, the PMO added.

Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, Sindh Food Minister Makhdoom Mehboob uz Zaman, and relevant senior officials also participated in the meeting, according to the statement.

During the meeting, the prime minister commended CM Maryam for “taking commendable steps such as farmers’ development, aquaculture, shrimp farming, and providing direct subsidies to farmers through the Kisan Card”.

The Sindh chief minister was also “working day and night for the development of farmers and providing them with facilities”, PM Shehbaz said, according to the statement.

The prime minister noted that the livestock sector also had vast potential to increase national exports, noting that measures were being taken to boost exports of Pakistani halal meat.

He added that the federal government would “provide all kinds of support to the provinces for the development of agriculture”.

“Providing fertilisers, quality seeds, modern machinery, and equipment and technical capabilities for better water utilisation to farmers at low cost is the top priority,” the prime minister said.

He added that ensuring fair prices to farmers for their crops, particularly small and medium-scale farmers, was a priority as well.

The Punjab chief minister and Sindh food minister shed light on the measures taken by the provincial governments for the development of farmers in their provinces, the PMO said.

It added that the briefings were also given at the meeting on measures for the development of agriculture in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, federal ministers Rana Tanveer Hussain, Dr Musadiq Malik, Jam Kamal Khan, Ahad Khan Cheema, Ahsan Iqbal, Attaullah Tarar, Khalid Hussain Magsi and Mian Moin Wattoo; and advisors Rana Sanaullah and Haroon Akhtar were among those who attended the meeting, according to the PMO.

In a meeting last week, National Food Security Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain said the targets for Rabi crops would befinalisedafter the “announcement of an illustrative price for wheat”.

“We are conscious of the challenges faced by our farmers due to rising input, energy and transportation costs,” the minister said.

Last month, the Pakistan Kissan Ittehaddemandeda Rs5,000 per 40kg support price for wheat, warning that farmers may not sow wheat for the next season if the government delays announcing crop policies.

The association had maintained that the farmers were unable to afford balanced fertiliser use because they were not recovering production costs.

In Sindh, Chief Minister Murad Ali Shahapprovedthe release of government wheat at the rate of Rs12,500 per 100kg bag from Oct 15 in order to stabilise flour prices and ensure its availability in the province.

Meanwhile, Punjab CM Maryam called an emergency meeting in response to rising flour prices, expressing strong displeasure over the increase, according to a PML-N post on X.

“The chief minister directed that affordable flour and wheat must be provided to the public under all circumstances,” the post said.

It added that a decision was made to increase the government-subsidised wheat quota for flour mills.

A subsidy of Rs10 billion was approved to ensure the availability of affordable flour, the PML-N said.

article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Pakistan’s economic growth at 3.5 per cent during the current fiscal year and inflation to remain close to double digits for another year, notwithstanding global growthrebounding to 3.4pc.

In its flagship World Economic Outlook,releasedat the launch of the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, the fund estimated Pakistan’s current account deficit to widen to 1pc of GDP from a surplus of 0.5pc in FY2025. Headline inflation is projected to rise significantly to 9.9pc from 7.1pc last year.

However, the Washington-based lending agency projected Pakistan’s unemployment rate to decline to 6.5pc this year, compared with 6.9pc last year and 7.1pc a year earlier.

The fund, which concluded its review of Pakistan’s economic situation last week, did not explain the projected decline in unemployment despite therising populationand its other economic forecasts, including higher inflation and a widening current account deficit.

The fund’s growth projections are significantly lower than the government’s 4pc target for the current year and the3.8pc forecastby the World Bank last month. Its estimated 3.5pc growth rate for Pakistan is slightly lower than the 3.6pc recorded last year but higher than the 3.2pc in FY2025.

Saying global economic activity had proved resilient despite multiple challenges, the international lender projected global growth to slow to 3.1pc in 2026 before rebounding to 3.4pc in 2027. Global headline inflation is projected to rise notably to 4.7pc in 2026 before easing to 4.1pc in 2027, it added.

The IMF attributed global economic resilience to the technology upturn, buffers and adaptations that helped mitigate the damage from geopolitics-driven disruptions.

“In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events. The pandemic and the ensuing disruptions to global supply chains; the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with the consequent sharp increases in the prices of energy and other commodities; and significant changes in trade barriers and trading relations have tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets, and governments,” it said.

“Individually, each of these major developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary. Yet, despite this barrage of shocks, the global economy has held up,” the IMF said.

It added that labour markets had remained unexpectedly strong, financial systems had broadly withstood the shocks and the sharpest monetary tightening in half a century, while inflation had receded from its peaks in many economies, although it remained persistent in some cases.

The IMF warned that energy-importing economies like Pakistan, which have limited links to the technology value chain, face the most difficult outlook. The margins of adjustment that have helped sustain resilience, however, are not limitless, and risks are skewed to the downside.

Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment ofexpectationssurrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth. On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI, or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could strengthen growth, it said.

The fund advised its members that fiscal frameworks must deliver better results in dealing with disruptive shocks and build policy space through revenue measures. During cost-of-living crises, governments should preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, it said.

The stable global aggregate masks a reallocation of growth across economies. Countries with limited direct exposure to the war shock and strong participation in the technology upturn are seeing activity hold up or strengthen. Energy exporters outside the immediate conflict zone are benefiting from favourable terms of trade.

Conversely, energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain face the most difficult combination of higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses.

Many low-income and vulnerable countries belong to this latter group, increasing the risk that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries.

The IMF projected world trade volume growth to slow in 2026 and stabilise in 2027, reflecting the drag from tariffs, adjustments in production chains and continued strength in technology-related trade.

Global imbalances are expected to decline only modestly over the medium term, as large fiscal deficits, limited domestic rebalancing, technology-driven capital flows and differing demand compositions across major economies under current policies continue to sustain external gaps.

The medium-term growth outlook remains lacklustre by historical standards and uneven across countries, partly reflecting varying degrees of AI preparedness and the robustness of energy mixes.

Risks are skewed to the downside, the IMF warned, adding that a prolonged stalemate or furtherescalation in the Middle Eastcould keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on growth.

Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyberattacks or extreme weather events could amplify these effects.

A day earlier, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb toldReutersthat the government expected the economy to growby more than 4pcthis fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. He also said the government was looking to privatise five to six entities during the year, potentially raising more than $1 billion.

Pakistan’s economy remains vulnerable to a prolonged conflict in the Middle East because of its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region.

headline: PM Shehbaz, EU official discuss Pakistan's efforts to curb migrant smuggling

importance Pakistan attaches to its partnership with the EU, according to a press release by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).The premier highlighted Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking through legislative reforms, institutional strengthening, effective enforcement and international cooperation.He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening cooperation across all pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.PM Shehbaz emphasised that efforts to address irregular migration should be complemented by practical opportunities for safe, orderly and regular migration.He noted that expanding legal pathways for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals would help meet the labour market needs of European countries while reducing prospective migrants’ vulnerability to smuggling networks.Brunner appreciated the measures taken and cooperation extended by the government of Pakistan, the PMO said.He expressed confidence that these efforts would contribute to expanding legal migration pathways and promoting mutually beneficial labour mobility between Pakistan and the European Union.President Zardari calls for more legal migration opportunitiesBrunner also called on President Asif Ali Zardari at the President’s House today, according to a two-part statement issued by the official presidential account on social media.“The meeting focused on Pakistan-EU relations, cooperation on migration management, efforts to combat human trafficking and migrant smuggling, and opportunities to facilitate legal migration,” the statement said.President Zardari called for greater opportunities for legal migration for Pakistani workers and professionals in Europe. He emphasised that Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration should be matched by “expanded legal pathways, skills-based mobility and structured cooperation” with the EU.He said that Pakistan attached great importance to its cooperation with the EU and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to implementing the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.The president highlighted the cooperation between the two countries in curbing irregular migration, noting that Pakistan continued to implement the EU Readmission Agreement and had readmitted more than 30,000 individuals over the years. He stressed the country’s commitment to combating human trafficking and irregular migration through “stronger legislation, institutional capacity, border controls and international cooperation”, the statement said.The president noted that, according to EU figures, irregular migration from Pakistan reduced by 64 per cent in the last 18 months, making it the only country in the region to achieve such a reduction. He said this progress reflected Pakistan’s “sustained efforts” and underlined the importance of expanding safe and legal avenues for migration.According to the president’s office, the meeting was informed that Pakistan had sought the EU’s assistance in strengthening the capacity of the Pakistan Coast Guards and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) to enhance efforts to combat irregular migration and migrant smuggling.“The president emphasised that legal migration pathways are essential to providing safe opportunities for workers and reducing reliance on smuggling networks,” the statement added.He highlighted the Pakistan-EU Migration and Mobility Dialogue as a “useful framework for matching Pakistan’s human-resource potential with European labour-market needs”, and expressed the hope that the next round of dialogue — expected to take place in Brussels early next year — would advance this cooperation.He expressed the country’s readiness to work with the EU on a structured mechanism to match its workforce with European labour-market requirements.President Zardari also welcomed the expansion of the EU Talent Partnerships framework and called for greater opportunities for skilled workers and professionals, including through circular migration.He expressed the hope that, given this partnership and the country’s efforts to curb irregular migration, the EU would consider establishing a European Legal Gateway Office in Pakistan.He said Pakistan and the EU have a “broad-based relationship spanning political dialogue, trade, development cooperation and other areas of mutual interest”, the statement added. He expressed confidence that continued engagement would strengthen mutual understanding and help advance practical cooperation on migration and mobility.Commissioner Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s role in maintaining regional balance and said Pakistan has done an “amazing job” in this regard, the statement noted.He also commended Pakistan’s efforts to prevent irregular migrants from undertaking dangerous journeys that cost many of them their lives.The commissioner was accompanied by EU Ambassador to Pakistan Raimundas Karoblis; Director for Migration and Home Affairs of the European Commission Henrik Nielsen; and member of Brunner’s cabinet, Grigorios Delavekouras.Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, Senator Sherry Rehman, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and former federal minister Naveed Qamar also attended the meeting, the statement added.Dar meets commissioner, highlights efforts to curb irregular migrationThe EU commissioner also met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad, during which the deputy premier highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking, the Foreign Office (FO) said.He stressed that these efforts should be complemented by greater opportunities for legal migration for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals.According to a statement issued by the FO, Dar expressed satisfaction with the positive momentum in Pakistan–EU relations.“The two sides discussed ways to strengthen cooperation on migration and mobility, a key pillar of the Pakistan–EU Strategic Engagement Plan (2019),” the FO said.It added that Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s progress in curbing irregular migration and noted the scope for expanding legal pathways for migration.Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening its partnership with the EU. He expressed the hope that Brunner’s visit would lead to “practical outcomes that benefit both sides”, the statement added.Naqvi, EU commissioner discuss border securitySeparately, Brunner also met with Interior Minister Naqvi in Islamabad, where they discussed enhancing cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management.The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks.Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable.He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration.Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration.“After a 64pc reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue.The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workers between Pakistan and the European Union.Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration.They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration.Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard.The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials.Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a64pc reductionin illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources.He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity.In February, Pakistan and three European countries — Italy, Spain and Greece — reached aconsensuson promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

He highlighted the Pakistan-EU Migration and Mobility Dialogue as a “useful framework for matching Pakistan’s human-resource potential with European labour-market needs”, and expressed the hope that the next round of dialogue — expected to take place in Brussels early next year — would advance this cooperation.

He expressed the country’s readiness to work with the EU on a structured mechanism to match its workforce with European labour-market requirements.

President Zardari also welcomed the expansion of the EU Talent Partnerships framework and called for greater opportunities for skilled workers and professionals, including through circular migration.

He expressed the hope that, given this partnership and the country’s efforts to curb irregular migration, the EU would consider establishing a European Legal Gateway Office in Pakistan.

He said Pakistan and the EU have a “broad-based relationship spanning political dialogue, trade, development cooperation and other areas of mutual interest”, the statement added. He expressed confidence that continued engagement would strengthen mutual understanding and help advance practical cooperation on migration and mobility.

Commissioner Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s role in maintaining regional balance and said Pakistan has done an “amazing job” in this regard, the statement noted.

He also commended Pakistan’s efforts to prevent irregular migrants from undertaking dangerous journeys that cost many of them their lives.

The commissioner was accompanied by EU Ambassador to Pakistan Raimundas Karoblis; Director for Migration and Home Affairs of the European Commission Henrik Nielsen; and member of Brunner’s cabinet, Grigorios Delavekouras.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry, Senator Sherry Rehman, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and former federal minister Naveed Qamar also attended the meeting, the statement added.

The EU commissioner also met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad, during which the deputy premier highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

He stressed that these efforts should be complemented by greater opportunities for legal migration for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals.

According to a statement issued by the FO, Dar expressed satisfaction with the positive momentum in Pakistan–EU relations.

“The two sides discussed ways to strengthen cooperation on migration and mobility, a key pillar of the Pakistan–EU Strategic Engagement Plan (2019),” the FO said.

It added that Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s progress in curbing irregular migration and noted the scope for expanding legal pathways for migration.

Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening its partnership with the EU. He expressed the hope that Brunner’s visit would lead to “practical outcomes that benefit both sides”, the statement added.

Separately, Brunner also met with Interior Minister Naqvi in Islamabad, where they discussed enhancing cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management.

The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks.

Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable.

He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration.

Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration.

“After a 64pc reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue.

The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workers between Pakistan and the European Union.

Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration.

They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration.

Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard.

The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials.

Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a64pc reductionin illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources.

He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity.

In February, Pakistan and three European countries — Italy, Spain and Greece — reached aconsensuson promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Tuesday that while low-income developing countries were dealing with the disproportionate impacts of theIran war-fuelled energy shock, many had “no choice” but to cut spending or potentially face debt restructuring.

Speaking toAFPon the sidelines of the organisation’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, IMF deputy director of research, Petya Koeva Brooks, said that the heavily indebted oil-importing countries were facing the worst of the energy shock, and had difficult choices in helping their citizens through the crisis.

“Unfortunately, after years of the global economy being hit [by] shock after shock, debt levels have increased quite a lot, and at the same time, inflation has become a problem,” she said.

TheUS war on Iranhas plunged the Middle East into conflict and sentglobal energy prices soaring, as Tehran’s retaliatory action targeted Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.

Those prices have begun to bleed into other goods, with the crisis also having an effect on crucial fertiliser supplies.

The IMF has called on countries to offer narrow, targeted subsidies in the wake of the crisis, while also recommending all governments work to rebuild fiscal buffers and address rising debt after years of fighting economic shocks since the pandemic.

“Our messages indeed apply to most countries, but again, the trade-offs and the choices that have to be made are much more difficult for the most vulnerable countries,” Koeva Brooks said.

The IMF’sWorld Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, identified low-income developing countries that are net oil importers and are not exposed to the ongoing artificial intelligence technology investment boom as being the most vulnerable to the shocks from the Iran war.

“For those countries that are most vulnerable, this is where the consumption basket is heavily weighted towards energy and food, and so indeed it is much much more difficult,” she said.

“But unfortunately there is no other choice.”

The senior IMF official added that “many” low-income countries were in debt distress, or close to it, and that they should seek debt restructuring if they were not able to address the issue.

“Where debt is not sustainable, then resolving that debt and having orderly and timely restructuring is always better than waiting, because then the cost of restructuring down the road is going to be much higher,” she said.

In its World Economic Outlook, the IMF raised its forecast for 2026 global growth, largely on the back of advanced economies enjoying a boost from AI-related investments and economic activity.

Growth outcomes were highly uneven across economies, depending on their exposure to the war and whether they were integrated into AI supply chains.

The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 per cent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.

Koeva Brooks toldAFPthat if AI investment activity were to slow, the world economy “would see a negative impact on output, not only in advanced countries like the US but again through trade linkages also in Asia”.

In the IMF’s worst-case scenario — of AI not delivering promised productivity gains — global GDP forecasts for 2028 would fall by as much as 0.4pc.

Climate-related risks were another key part of the World Economic Outlook this year, and Koeva Brooks toldAFPthat some of the effects of a particularly intense El Niño phenomenon had already been taken into account in higher prices for certain food items.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Niño raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.

“We have a significant increase in beverage prices, in the prices of rice, and so on,” said Koeva Brooks.

“Of course, it could turn out that the domino effect is even bigger than what we currently have.”

The government on Monday reduced the price of petrol by Rs2.93 per litre, but increased that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Re0.61 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs395.37 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.85 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 13 (Tuesday).

The price of HSD has come down from apeak of Rs520.35recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price hadpeaked at Rs458.41on April 3 after beginning itsupward trajectoryfrom Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government hasreintroduceda raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malikannouncedthat fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcingweekly revisionsto fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April alsoannouncedtargeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Sheh­baz Sharif on Monday directed the auth­orities to increase financing for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from Rs1.1 trillion to Rs2.2tr by 2028, citing their potential to drive economic growth and create business opportunities across the country.

Presiding over a meeting on the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority (Smeda), the prime minister said the business community was the backbone of any country’s economy, while Pakistan’s SME sector had imme­nse potential to accelerate economic dev­elopment, according to a press release issued by the Prime Minister’s Office.

He said ongoing reforms at Smeda ai­­m­­ed to empower small and medium-siz­­ed entrepreneurs and facilitate the esta­blishment and expansion of businesses.

The prime minister emphasised the need to empower people in underdeveloped areas, saying this would help red­uce migration to major cities and contribute to balanced national development.

PM Shehbaz directed Smeda to formulate a comprehensive plan to educate more people about the procedures for obtaining business loans and take effective measures to raise awareness about entrepreneurship.

Feasibility studies

He also instructed the authority to commission feasibility studies for setting up SMEs in various sectors with the help of relevant industry experts and make them available in local languages. The initiative, he said, would enable aspiring entrepreneurs across the country to benefit from the studies.

During the meeting, the prime minister was briefed on ongoing reforms at Smeda and measures to promote the SME sector.

The meeting was informed that Smeda was being transformed into a central platform to train aspiring entrepreneurs and facilitate their access to bank financing for setting up businesses.

Smeda offices were being established across the country to improve outreach and access to services, while the authority was developing an artificial intelligence-based helpline to provide information and guidance to citizens in local languages. The meeting was also informed that a memorandum of understanding had been signed between global e-commerce company Alibaba and Smeda under which 10,000 SMEs would receive training over two years.

Officials said reforms were also under way to improve the effectiveness and user-friendliness of Smeda’s digital portal.

Daanish IT Park

At a separate meeting, PM Shehbaz directed the authorities concerned to develop the Daanish IT Park Islamabad into a world-class technology hub and a centre for a modern IT ecosystem through effective collaboration between academia and industry.

He said the government would continue efforts to equip Pakistani youth with modern skills in information technology, artificial intelligence and financial technology, while creating new opportunities for IT entrepreneurs.

He instructed the Ministry of Information Technology to conduct a comprehensive case study of the project and directed the authorities to make the IT park operational in partnership with global technology companies. He also ordered a third-party audit of the project.

The meeting was briefed on plans to create a comprehensive ecosystem to boost IT exports and promote investment in the sector. It was informed that 50 privately owned buildings had been upgraded into software technology parks under the Pakistan Software Export Board.

Additionally, eight incubation centres had been established across the country to support start-ups, while 105 co-working spaces were operational to facilitate IT professionals.

Participants were told that global technology companies were being approached to help operationalise the Daanish IT Park Islamabad.

article_text:
WASHINGTON: More than one-third of Pakistan’s population faces overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards, according to the United Nations Development Prog­ramme’s (UNDP) Multidimensional Pov­er­ty Index (MPI) released on Monday.

Figures released by the UNDP in New York show that 38.3 per cent of Pakistan’s population was multidimensionally poor, compared with 16.4 per cent in India and 14.9pc in Bangladesh. The estimates are based on household surveys conducted in different years and do not provide a strictly contemporaneous comparison.

In Pakistan, the intensity of deprivation among those classified as multidimensionally poor stood at 51.7pc. Another 12.9pc of the population was considered vulnerable to multidimensional poverty, indicating that a substantial share of people remained at risk of falling into acute deprivation.

Unlike conventional income-based measures, the MPI assesses overlapping disadvantages in areas such as nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing and household assets.

UNDP estimates 38.3pc Pakistanis face multidimensional poverty

The report also documents a worrying global reversal. The number of people living in multidimensional poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.

The latest total is 51.5 million higher than the previous update. Children account for more than half of those affected, with 617m living in multidimensional poverty, while 83pc of the total live in rural areas.

The global findings underline the scale of the challenge facing governments, particularly in providing essential services to disadvantaged communities. Poverty is not simply a shortage of income; it can also mean inadequate nutrition, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity.

South Asia accounts for a substantial share of global deprivation. The report says the region accounts for at least one-third of global deprivations in nutrition, housing, and years of schooling.

It is also home to 150m poor people living in households where a school-aged child is not attending school, highlighting persistent barriers to education despite broader development gains.

The UNDP’s regional figures put South Asia’s multidimensional poverty rate at approximately 19.3pc, with another 18.4pc of the population vulnerable to such poverty. Health accounts for about 29.9pc of the contribution to regional multidimensional poverty, education for 33.7pc and living standards for 36.3pc.

The figures show how disadvantages in different areas reinforce one another. Poor health, inadequate education and substandard living conditions can trap families in poverty and make it difficult for them to improve their circumstances.

“The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.

“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.”

KARACHI: The imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in PTI-ruled Khyber Pakhtunkhwa further weakened already fragile investor sentiment on Monday. The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) remained under pressure from Middle East tensions, elevated oil and petroleum prices, inflationary pressures and political instability, all contributing to continued economic uncertainty.

As a result, the market remained under unrelenting selling pressure, dragging the benchmark KSE-100 index below the 166,000 level.

Despite a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund that paved the way for the release of $1.2 billion under the two ongoing programmes, subject to executive board approval, it failed to support the market in recent days.

Oil prices rose to near two-week highs as attacks on Saudi Arabia overshadowed the possibility of further supplies to the market. Brent crude futures rose $2.07, or 2pc, to $106.79, their highest since Sept 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.54 a barrel, up $1.69, or 1.8pc.

Index tumbles 1,964 points on aggressive selling

Topline Securities Ltd said the index came under renewed selling pressure, plunging 1,920 points intraday before closing at 165,124.41, down 1,964.87 points, or 1.18 per cent.

Bearish sentiment followed the federal government’s decision to impose an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa after President Asif Ali Zardari approved the federal cabinet’s recommendation on Sunday. The development heightened political uncertainty, prompting investors to adopt a cautious stance amid concerns about the evolving situation.

The announcement further dampened investor sentiment, triggering broad-based selling as market participants stayed on the sidelines amid heightened uncertainty and a lack of fresh positive catalysts.

United Bank, Oil and Gas Development Company, Habib Bank, Meezan Bank, and Lucky Cement emerged as the major laggards, collectively shaving approximately 645 points off the KSE-100 Index.

Investor participation remained subdued, well below the 500-million-share level, though total trading volume rose 17.3pc to 362.95m shares over the weekend session and turnover value rose 6.02pc to Rs14.5bn. Treet Corpo­ration led the volume chart with 27m shares.

Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said the PSX recorded a bearish, volatile session as the market opened lower amid heightened domestic political uncertainty.

However, value buying at lower levels provided some support, triggering a brief recovery in the be_nchmark index. Never­the­less, the rebound proved short-lived, and the market closed firmly lower.

He said the market was likely to remain volatile amid heightened domestic political uncertainty and cautious investor sentiment. Further downside pressure cannot be ruled out, although value buying at lower levels may provide intermittent support. He advised investors to remain selective, prioritise fundamentally strong stocks, and avoid aggressive positions until sentiment stabilises.

ISLAMABAD: The government said on Monday it had to cut the foreign-funded project portfolio by more than half, from Rs537 billion to Rs255bn, due to a shortage of matching funds in local currency for the current fiscal year.

This was reported to the Senate Standing Committee on Planning, Development and Special Initiatives by a team led by Planning Secretary Dr Tahir Noor.

Mr Noor also informed the committee that work on the Sukkur-Hyderabad (M6) Motorway would begin “within months” as foreign financing totalling $705 million was now available.

The meeting, presided over by Senator Quratulain Marri, reviewed allocations for foreign-funded development projects under PSDP 2026–27.

The panel was informed that 98 foreign-funded projects, with a total estimated cost of Rs8.1 trillion, were included in the current fiscal year’s PSDP, involving foreign assistance of Rs4.65tr.

Against a demand of Rs537bn for rupee cover, the Economic Affairs Division (EAD) had proposed Rs425bn after consultation with the ministries, divisions and donor agencies concerned. However, the National Economic Council (NEC), while approving the PSDP at Rs1tr against an overall demand of Rs2.9tr on June 10, allocated only Rs255bn for these projects due to fiscal constraints.

Senator Marri sought clarification regarding projects expected to be completed during the current financial year. The planning team reported that most of the projects were expected to be completed during the year.

The Senate committee emphasised effective monitoring and timely implementation to achieve projected targets for projects that were now at an advanced stage.

While reviewing the need for reliance on foreign loans, particularly dollar-denominated financing carrying interest and repayment obligations, the panel was of the view that priority should be given to domestic resources and rupee allocations because foreign borrowing had financial implications and needed to be carefully assessed. The government should explore the effective utilisation of local resources to reduce unnecessary dependence on external loans, the panel observed.

The committee was of the view that foreign-funded projects must receive adequate rupee cover to avoid implementation delays, while ensuring transparency, accountability, prudent financial management and coordination with donor agencies.

It emphasised balancing foreign as­­sis­tance with domestic fiscal capacity and mi­­nimising avoidable financial burdens.

The meeting reviewed progress on the Sukkur–Hyderabad Motorway project and expressed concern over prolonged delays. The committee was told that Sections I and II were being processed under the public-private partn­ership (PPP) mode, with the concession award targeted for February next year.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has agreed to provide transaction advisory services for these sections.

In addition, financing arrangements with international development partners had been secured for the remaining sections, the planning ministry reported.

ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday directed the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to complete the digital monitoring system of sales production in major industries by the end of December, as part of efforts to narrow the gap between actual and potential tax collection.

Chairing a meeting in Islamabad to review FBR reforms, the premier instructed tax authorities to ensure production monitoring for sales tax across all manufacturing sectors by the year end, an official statement said.

It added that officials gave a detailed presentation to the premier on the results achieved so far from the industries already under the monitoring system.

The meeting was informed that the digital monitoring system had been fully installed in sugar, cement, tobacco, tiles and fertilisers sectors. The monitoring system was in the process of being installed in the textile, packaged water, packaged juice, and packaged milk sectors, and the purchase of equipment for this purpose had been completed, the meeting was told.

It was further informed that the purchase of equipment for the sectors of steel, poultry, and tires will be completed by Oct 15, while for tea, household electronics, leather, paper and board, and oil and ghee, the purchase will be completed by Oct 30.

As a result, the monitoring systems in all these production sectors are expected to be fully operational by Dec 31, it was told.

The meeting was informed that in the textile sector, some industries had shown resistance to the installation of the monitoring system. However, Nishat Mills, Al-Karam Textile, Al-Karam Cotton Mills, J.K. Spinning Mills, Soorti Enterprises, Interloop Limited, Faisal Spinning Mills, Ibrahim Fibers Limited, Sapphire Textiles Limited and Nishat Chunian had voluntarily installed the monitoring system in compliance with government measures.

PM Shehbaz appreciated these companies for their cooperation.

A review report on the gap between actual and potential tax collection was also presented to the premier, which provided an estimate of the country’s tax potential and assessed additional revenue that could potentially be generated via improved tax compliance and enforcement.

The meeting was informed that due to government measures over the past three years, an additional Rs1.3 trillion in tax had beencollected— a 40 per cent increase in tax collection. This additional tax was collected due to enforcement measures, it was told.

During its briefing, the FBR said that production monitoring was being made effective with the help of cameras under the faceless system.

“The prime minister directed the removal of all hurdles in the installation of automated production monitoring systems,” the statement said.

He also noted that businesses collecting and pocketing taxes from consumers themselves instead of depositing it into the national exchequer were not entitled to any concessions.

The premier said that those businesses in the production sector that were voluntarily installing the monitoring system were viewed with appreciation. He added that all necessary measures would be taken to achieve the country’s “full tax potential” and ensure effective enforcement of tax laws.

He commended the FBR Transformation Team for its “round-the-clock efforts” in preparing the comprehensive assessment and identifying the gap between potential revenue and actual collection. He also appreciated the officials involved in preparing the report, presenting them with shields after the meeting.

The prime minister said that to assess the effectiveness of the production monitoring system, the IT ministry should also conduct audits in other sectors. He termed the collection of tax in accordance with the country’s full tax potential a “true service to the public”.

The meeting was attended by Federal Ministers Azam Nazeer Tarar, Dr Musadik Malik, Ahad Khan Cheema and Shaza Fatima Khawaja, as well as Minister of State Bilal Azhar Kayani, Advisor to the Prime Minister Haroon Akhtar, and relevant senior officials.

The government is looking to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of $1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb toldReuterson Monday, stating that he expected the economy to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices.

Pakistan’s economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

Pakistan has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said.

“So I’m still quite clear that we should clock north of4pc,” he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annualmeetingsof the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.

“And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices.”

Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a $7bn, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income.

Following theprivatisationof flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations.

“I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year,” he said, adding that they could raise more than $1bn.

Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan’s reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances.

“We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country,” said Aurangzeb. “So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem.”

The US-Israeli-ledwarwith Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years.

Pakistan, whichreacheda staff-level agreement with the IMF last week, potentially unlocking about $1.21bn in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed $10bn exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said.

But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations.

“If it comes through, this will be a great help for us,” he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States and the US International Development Finance Corporation.

“If it doesn’t come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market.”

article_text:
Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilise disruptive economic fluctuations.

The two were honoured for developing new models for managing recessions and other crises that fail to respond to traditional tools.

“On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the jury said.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained in a statement that ever since John Maynard Keynes formulated his economic theories almost a century ago, “stabilisation” policies had long let officials boost economic growth when needed.

But during the oil shocks in the 1970s, the Keynesian models that governed when and how action should be taken no longer worked.

Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University born in 1955, separately began to explore new models.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the jury said.

Hall and Woodford’s models include an “understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions”, it said.

A fundamental aspect of this is the understanding that households are forward-looking when making decisions about spending or saving.

This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence people’s views of the future when making such decisions.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

“It’s a surprise, but I’m feeling very good about it,” Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt “elated” for receiving “a tremendous honour”.

While his theories have had a large impact on policymakers, he said they had not been “motivated by a specific political agenda”.

“It was an attempt to improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy and therefore to contribute both to the management of the economy, but also to contribute to public understanding,” Woodford said.

The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.

It was instead created through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.

But like the Nobels inchemistryandphysics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.

Last year, theeconomics awardwent to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.

Last week, South African judgeNavi Pillaywon the peace prize, and Canadian-Icelandic writerAnne Carsonwas named the literature laureate.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry wasawardedto Frenchman Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai of Japan, and the Physics Prize to BelgianFrancis Halzen.

And the first prize to be announced, inmedicine, went to American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.

Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.

The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.

headline: Textile makers warn of steep decline in exports from Oct to Dec
summary: • Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation cites weak Western demand, higher freight, rising production costs• Exporters seek 6-8pc Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies support, clearance of outstanding refunds• Industry says announced 4.5pc Export Finance Scheme rate yet to be implementedISLAMABAD: Textile exporters have warned the government of a steep decline in goods exports during the second quarter (October-December) of the current fiscal year, citing weakening demand in Wes­tern markets, rising freight charges and escalating production costs.In a statement issued on Sunday, Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation (PTEA) Patron-in-Chief Khur­ram Mukhtar said the country’s export sector was facing mounting pressure from multiple directions, threatening its competitiveness and share in international markets.He said inflation in Western markets had weakened dem­and from international buyers, while sea freight charges had increased by 1.5 to 2.5 times, squeezing exporters’ already thin profit margins.Rising input and logistics costs were further undermining the competitiveness of Pakistani products, he added.“The decline in export trade volume is unprecedented,” Mr Mukhtar said, warning that only financially strong exporters would survive the prevailing conditions. He cautioned that regaining lost market share would be extremely difficult.He said declining exports were affecting the entire textile value chain, including ginning, spinning, weaving, processing and knitting. The situation had been compounded by weak domestic demand amid high inflation, putting several segments of the industry under severe financial pressure.Mr Mukhtar urged the government to provide temporary support thro­ugh the Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme at a rate of 6pc to 8pc to help exporters ret­ain their international market share. • Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation cites weak Western demand, higher freight, rising production costs• Exporters seek 6-8pc Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies support, clearance of outstanding refunds• Industry says announced 4.5pc Export Finance Scheme rate yet to be implemented

ISLAMABAD: Textile exporters have warned the government of a steep decline in goods exports during the second quarter (October-December) of the current fiscal year, citing weakening demand in Wes­tern markets, rising freight charges and escalating production costs.

In a statement issued on Sunday, Pakistan Textile Exporters Associ­ation (PTEA) Patron-in-Chief Khur­ram Mukhtar said the country’s export sector was facing mounting pressure from multiple directions, threatening its competitiveness and share in international markets.

He said inflation in Western markets had weakened dem­and from international buyers, while sea freight charges had increased by 1.5 to 2.5 times, squeezing exporters’ already thin profit margins.

Rising input and logistics costs were further undermining the competitiveness of Pakistani products, he added.

“The decline in export trade volume is unprecedented,” Mr Mukhtar said, warning that only financially strong exporters would survive the prevailing conditions. He cautioned that regaining lost market share would be extremely difficult.

He said declining exports were affecting the entire textile value chain, including ginning, spinning, weaving, processing and knitting. The situation had been compounded by weak domestic demand amid high inflation, putting several segments of the industry under severe financial pressure.

Mr Mukhtar urged the government to provide temporary support thro­ugh the Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme at a rate of 6pc to 8pc to help exporters ret­ain their international market share. He also demanded immediate clearance of outstanding refunds under various heads to ease the liquidity crisis across the textile supply chain and called for the removal of cross-subsidies embedded in industrial energy tariffs to reduce production costs.

Highlighting anomalies in the Export Finance Scheme (EFS), he said the government had announced a fixed financing rate of 4.5pc in the FY27 Finance Bill, but the decision had yet to be implemented.

According to him, banks were charging exporters a minimum of 5.5pc, while some were charging as much as 8.5pc, contrary to the announced rate.

Mr Mukhtar claimed that around Rs200 billion in financing had been extended under the EFS to yarn exporters despite yarn being on the scheme’s negative list. He also questioned the provision of financing to sugar exporters, describing sugar as a highly regulated sector.

In contrast, he said, eligible textile exporters whose export performance exceeded the State Bank of Pakistan’s mandatory requirement by a substantial margin were being denied financing allocations.

He said some exporters were achieving five to six times the requi­red export performance against the mandatory threshold of two times, yet were unable to obtain financing.

Such allocations, he argued, discouraged value addition and penalised exporters contributing significantly to the country’s foreign exchange earnings.

Mr Mukhtar welcomed the incre­ase in EFS financing allocations for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) but questioned whether the additional funds could be effectively utilised.

He said an additional Rs300bn allocation for SMEs would require export performance of Rs600bn, which, according to him, did not currently exist. He pointed out that the Rs100bn allocation for SMEs in the previous fiscal year had lapsed without being utilised. He urged the government to review the distribution of EFS financing according to the export contribution of each segment, arguing that the top 100 exporters accounted for up to 60pc of total export volume and should receive proportionate financing.

To strengthen the textile supply chain, Mr Mukhtar proposed a targeted financing pac­kage of Rs140bn for modernisation and technological upgrading of four major segments.

The proposed package incl­udes Rs20bn each for ginning and sizing, and Rs50bn each for weaving and processing.

He said these sectors required specially designed short- and long-term financing facilities for balancing, modernisation and replacement of machinery, improving productivity and introducing automation and sustainable production practices.

Mr Mukhtar said the federal government and the State Bank should jointly develop the proposed financing programme in consultation with industry representatives.

He also called for a 10-year strategic plan for textile exp­orts, focusing on Pakistan’s exis­ting industrial expertise, exportable surplus and structural reforms needed to impr­ove international competitiveness.

“Historically, we have been reactive. The current situation demands a proactive appro­ach,” he said, warning that timely intervention would cost considerably less than efforts to recover lost export markets.

headline: The influencer economy relies on advertisers borrowing the influencer’s credibility
summary: https://www.dawn.com/news/2036550
relevant_sector_or_market: AUTOMOBILE | ECONOMY & MACRO | MISCELLANEOUS | TECHNOLOGY & TELECOM
article_text:
The advertising business in Pakistan is undergoing a fundamental change. For decades, marketing was relatively straightforward. A company launched a product, appointed an advertising agency, produced a television commercial, bought airtime, put up billboards and perhaps hired a celebrity as its brand ambassador. The consumer has moved.

The advertising rupee is beginning to follow. Pakistan now has around 80 million adult social-media user identities. TikTok alone has an advertising reach approaching 80m adults, while YouTube reaches around 54m and Instagram around 22m. More importantly, Pakistanis are spending increasing amounts of their media time on these platforms.This has created a new industry: the influencer economy.

Consider the numbers. Jannat Mirza has over 25m followers on TikTok. Ducky Bhai has over 10m YouTube subscribers. Rajab Butt’s family channel has around 9m. Hania Aamir has crossed 20m followers on Instagram.

There are then thousands of smaller influencers specialising in fashion, food, beauty, technology, travel, gaming, automobiles and financial services. Why should companies care?

Content creators themselves will become businesses employing videographers, editors, and sales teams

Because advertising has historically been about renting somebody else’s audience. A brand paid a television channel because the channel had viewers. It paid a newspaper because the newspaper had readers. It paid for a billboard because people drove past it.

An influencer also owns an audience. The difference is that the relationship with that audience can be considerably more personal. If a television commercial tells me a restaurant serves excellent food, I know I am watching an advertisement. If someone whose food reviews I watch every week visits the restaurant and recommends a particular dish, the communication is different. The advertiser is effectively borrowing the influencer’s credibility.

Influencers get paid in several ways. The simplest is a fixed payment for a post, reel or video. Smaller influencers may receive a few thousand rupees or simply free products. Established creators can charge tens or hundreds of thousands of rupees. Celebrity influencers can command considerably more.

But the more interesting models are performance-based. An influencer can receive a commission for every product sold through a unique link or promotional code. Instead of paying Rs1m for an advertisement and hoping consumers buy the product, the company can pay according to actual sales.

Thus, advertising is becoming measurable distribution. Imagine a clothing company working with 100 influencers. Each receives a different promotional code. Within days, the company knows that influencer A generated 500 sales, Influencer B generated 50 and Influencer C generated none. The next marketing budget practically allocates itself. This also changes the economics for small businesses.

A new Pakistani cosmetics brand cannot compete with multinational spending but it can identify 50 beauty influencers whose followers match its target customer, send them products and compensate them partly on sales.

It also explains why follower count is becoming less important. An influencer with 50,000 followers interested in motorcycles may be more valuable to a motorcycle manufacturer than an entertainer with 5m followers. The question is not how many people follow you. It is whether they are the people I want to sell to — and whether they buy.

The next stage is live commerce. China has demonstrated how powerful the combination of influencers, entertainment and e-commerce can become. The influencer does not simply advertise a product. He or she demonstrates it live, answers questions, creates urgency and allows the customer to purchase immediately.

Pakistan has most of the ingredients required: smartphones, social media, digital payments, e-commerce logistics and, most importantly, a young population comfortable buying through a screen. An influencer can therefore move from being an advertiser to becoming a retailer. However, there are risks.

The first is transparency. Consumers frequently cannot distinguish between an independent recommendation and paid promotion. If an influencer is compensated that relationship should be disclosed. This becomes particularly important when influencers promote financial or health products. Trust cannot become a substitute for consumer protection.

The second problem is fake influence. Followers can be purchased, views can be generated, and engagement can be manufactured. Companies therefore need to stop measuring influencer marketing primarily through followers and start measuring it through customer acquisition cost, engagement, conversion and repeat purchases.This will also professionalise the industry.

Pakistan will increasingly see influencer agencies, talent managers, analytics companies, affiliate networks and technology platforms connecting brands with creators. Influencers themselves will become businesses employing videographers, editors, researchers and sales teams.

Traditional advertising will not disappear. Television remains powerful, billboards work, celebrity endorsements will continue, but the monopoly has disappeared. A Pakistani with a smartphone can now build an audience larger than many traditional media properties without owning a television station, printing press or an advertising agency.

And once you own the audience, you own something advertisers want. Pakistan’s next important retail channel may not be a shopping mall, television station or e-commerce website. It may simply be someone you follow.

article_text:
The apparent transformation of rural society sits uneasily with the landed elite’s strong presence in Pakistan’s legislatures, pointing to a disconnect between landownership patterns and political representation.

Does this reflect limitations in the sample-based Agriculture Census, ambiguities in legislators’ self-declared professions, or the disproportionate political influence of a relatively small landed class? How does this group continue to outnumber — and potentially outmanoeuvre — other professional categories in assemblies?

Across national and provincial legislatures, landowners and those with agri-business interests emerged as the largest professional group, based on members’ self-declarations to the Election Commission of Pakistan. This contrasts sharply with the changing rural landscape: official data show increasingly fragmented landholdings, with barely three per cent of farmers owning more than 12.5 acres.

Understanding legislators’ composition, backgrounds, and interests is essential to assess political and economic policy choices objectively. In Pakistan’s complex, multi-ethnic society, however, a vast informal sector, weak data collection, public mistrust and misreporting make this difficult. Limited access to official records has further constrained systemic research.

Many political leaders belong to the 3pc of farmers holding more than 12.5 acres

The Free and Fair Election Network (Fafen) Parliament Monitor on the 15th National Assembly 2018-2023, based on Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) data, is perhaps the most comprehensive study of legislators’ professional backgrounds. According to Fafen, a similar analysis of the current legislatures is under preparation but has been delayed by the ECP’s slow provision of legislators’ declarations. Repeated attempts to seek the ECP’s input for this article were unsuccessful.

Of the total 1,058 legislators in the 2018 National Assembly and four provincial assemblies, 432 declared agriculture as their profession, far exceeding 223 businessmen, 81 full-time politicians, 49 lawyers, 25 doctors and 19 educationists, among others. Agriculturists accounted for 172 of 330 members of the National Assembly, 131 of 371 in Punjab, 76 of 168 in Sindh, 32 of 124 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 21 of 65 in Balochistan.

Shahid Khaqan Abbasi, former prime minister, businessman and senior leader of Awaam Pakistan, attributed the apparent disconnect to elite capture. “Members of the national and provincial assemblies, senators and political leaders largely belong to the 3pc of farmers holding more than 12.5 acres. They use their influence to control additional ‘benami’ land registered in the names of relatives, employees, servants or haris, secure government land on lease and obtain private land on concessional terms for cultivation by tenants.

“More importantly, many elite farmers derive substantial income from corruption and undeclared or illegal businesses, using agriculture income to launder earnings and evade taxes,” he alleged. “Besides, actually a large part of our elite uses ‘farming income’ to avoid taxes. The government does not ask how X acres of land can generate RsY of income. Everybody you meet will tell you, I have a ‘farm’. These are basically expensive, palatial homes built on farmland, and used to justify ‘farm’ income.”

Mr Abbasi argued that agricultural income also provides a convenient tax shelter for the wider elite. “Nobody questions how a given acreage can generate a declared level of income. Almost everyone claims to own a farm, often a palatial residence built on agricultural land, which is then used to justify supposedly agricultural earnings.”

Ziad Bashir, CEO of Ideas and a prominent business leader, argues that the apparent contradiction between 97pc of farmers operating less than 12.5 acres and agriculture dominating legislators’ declared professions may reflect different realities. Genuine fragmentation occurs through inheritance, while the census captures operational holdings, including tenancies, rather than simply ownership. But formal records may also understate effective control when family members or associates divide land while managing it as a single farm.

“Technology could help test this. Satellite imagery can identify adjoining parcels that show common cropping, irrigation, and harvesting patterns. Overlaying these with digitised land records and, under appropriate legal safeguards, ownership, family, utility, credit and crop-payment data could reveal who actually controls an agricultural operation. The constraint is therefore less technological than institutional: improving land records, data integration, transparency and political commitment.”

Dr Usama Ehsan Khan, an IBA researcher, stated that the apparent contradiction reflects two different measures. The Agriculture Census captures farm structure, overwhelmingly dominated by small holdings, while Fafen records legislators’ self-declared professions, revealing nothing about acreage owned. The real divide, therefore, is between the numerical dominance of small farmers and the disproportionate political influence associated with landed wealth.

Tax policy reinforces this dynamic. Agricultural income, taxed provincially, has historically enjoyed lighter taxation than comparable non-agricultural income, although recent reforms seek greater parity. Weak enforcement, combined with unequal landownership, patronage and access to state institutions, helps sustain landed influence despite continuing fragmentation of farms through inheritance.

Mehmood Nawaz Shah, president of the Sindh Abadgar Board, said the apparent disconnect raises two issues: the reliability of the census data and the fact that even if only 3pc of farmers own larger holdings, that pool is still sizeable enough to account for the strong presence of agriculturists in the assemblies.

A Lahore-based expert argued that agriculture has historically provided a convenient avenue for income-tax avoidance in Pakistan. Despite provincial legislation to tax agricultural income, enforcement remains weak, compounded by poor documentation of farm output and productivity.

Citing some 17,000 farms of 100 acres or more, he pointed to absentee landlords who lease land in smaller parcels to tenants or contractors. He argued that such earnings should be taxed like other rental income but often escape scrutiny. Shared ownership further complicates matters when one family member manages the entire holding without declaring the proceeds as personal taxable income.

Independent analyst Rashid Chaudhry argued that legislators often declare agriculture as their profession for tax advantages, although declining profitability makes it unlikely to be their principal income source. He said cotton’s collapse, repeated crop losses, and market crashes have undermined farming’s commercial viability.

Calling the sample-based Agriculture Census merely indicative, Mr Chaudhry questioned how much land the largest 3pc actually control, noting that land reforms remain stalled and individual holdings face no effective ceiling.

The writer is a former Dawn staffer
